titulo: Will artificial intelligence hollow out white-collar jobs?

fuente.nota: Escrito para el panel de idiomas. Los datos son aproximados y no deben citarse como fuente.

parrafos: Every technological revolution arrives with its own prophecy of doom. The power loom was supposed to impoverish weavers for ever; the computer was meant to abolish the office clerk. Now it is the turn of generative artificial intelligence, and this time the anxiety has moved up the social ladder. It is no longer factory hands who lie awake at night, but lawyers, accountants, translators and the legions of analysts who populate the glass towers of our financial districts. Are their fears justified? Partly, I would argue, but not in the way most people imagine.

Let us begin with what is genuinely new. Previous waves of automation mostly replaced manual tasks, or routine cognitive ones that could be reduced to explicit rules: sorting, calculating, filing. Large language models do something different. They draft contracts, summarise reports, write software and answer customer queries in fluent prose. In other words, they encroach on precisely the kind of non-routine, language-based work that economists once considered safe, and that has underpinned the expansion of the middle class in advanced economies for the best part of half a century.

The exposure is therefore considerable. Most estimates suggest that a large share of the tasks performed in professional occupations, perhaps a quarter or more, could in principle be carried out or assisted by current systems. Clerical and administrative roles appear the most vulnerable, followed by jobs in finance, law and marketing. Unlike earlier forms of automation, which hit the lower rungs of the wage distribution hardest, this one seems to bear down on the middle and even the upper-middle, on precisely those graduates who were told that a degree was the surest insurance against obsolescence.

Yet exposure is not the same as destruction. A task that can be automated is not a job that disappears. Most occupations are bundles of tasks, some of which a machine performs better and others which still require judgement, trust or a human face. When spreadsheets arrived in the 1980s, many predicted the demise of the bookkeeper; instead, the number of accountants grew, because cheaper analysis created an appetite for more of it. Economists call this the price elasticity of demand, and it remains the great unknown of the whole debate.

There is also the stubborn reality of adoption. Firms do not overhaul their organisation the moment a new tool becomes available. They must redesign processes, retrain staff, clean up their data and satisfy regulators, all of which takes years, if not decades. Electricity took roughly a generation to transform factory productivity. Early surveys of companies experimenting with AI paint a strikingly similar picture: enthusiasm in the boardroom, patchy results on the ground, and productivity gains that are real but unevenly spread. Many workers, meanwhile, use the tools quietly on their own initiative, long before their employers have decided on any strategy.

None of this, however, should lull us into complacency. The more plausible danger is not mass unemployment but a hollowing-out of career ladders. Junior tasks, the drafting, the background research, the first-pass analysis, are exactly what AI does well, and they are also how young professionals learn their trade. If firms saw off the bottom rungs, they may save money today only to discover tomorrow that nobody is ready to step into senior positions. The apprenticeship on which professional life has always rested could quietly erode.

Distribution is the second concern. Early studies suggest that AI assistants raise the productivity of less experienced workers the most, narrowing the gap between novices and veterans within a firm. That is encouraging. But the gains between firms, and between workers and owners, may run the other way. If a handful of technology companies capture most of the value, and if employers pocket the savings rather than share them, the result could be stagnant wages for the many and windfall profits for the few.

What, then, should policymakers do? Resisting the technology would be futile and probably self-defeating; Europe already lags behind the United States and China in developing it. The wiser course is to shape its diffusion. That means investing heavily in adult education, not in short courses of dubious value, but in serious retraining linked to real vacancies. It means rethinking social insurance so that mid-career workers can switch occupation without sliding into poverty. And it means a competition policy vigilant enough to stop a few platforms from becoming gatekeepers.

Employers bear their share of responsibility too. The temptation to treat AI purely as a cost-cutting device is understandable, especially when shareholders are impatient. Yet firms that use it instead to augment their staff, freeing them from tedious chores to spend more time with clients or on genuinely complex problems, are likely to fare better in the long run. As one senior manager put it to me, the question is not how many people the machine can replace, but what those people could achieve if the machine did the dull part of their job.

As for workers themselves, the advice is less glamorous than the headlines. The skills that complement AI rather than compete with it are, by and large, old-fashioned ones: judgement, negotiation, the ability to explain complex matters to non-specialists and the willingness to take responsibility for a decision. Paradoxically, the professions most threatened by the new technology may well be rescued by the most human of their attributes, the very qualities that no amount of computing power has so far managed to imitate convincingly.

So will artificial intelligence hollow out white-collar work? It will certainly reshape it, and some jobs will undoubtedly vanish, as typists and switchboard operators did before them. But history suggests that the outcome is not written in the code. It will depend on choices made in parliaments, boardrooms and classrooms over the coming decade, and on whether the productivity dividend is broadly shared. Technology widens the range of possible futures; it does not choose among them. The machines are not the ones deciding. We are.
titulo_es: ¿Vaciará la inteligencia artificial los empleos de oficina?
resumen_es: Tribuna de opinión sobre el efecto de la IA generativa en los empleos cualificados: el autor sostiene que el riesgo no es el paro masivo sino la desaparición de los puestos de entrada y el reparto desigual de las ganancias, y propone respuestas de política pública.

ideas_clave.idea: Fear of automation, once a concern of manual workers, has now spread to highly qualified professionals, and the author considers it only partly justified.
Unlike earlier technologies, language models can perform non-routine intellectual work, so a significant part of professional and middle-income tasks is exposed.
Being exposed does not mean being destroyed, since jobs combine many tasks and cheaper services may increase demand, as happened with accountants after spreadsheets.
Companies adopt new technologies slowly, so productivity gains from AI are so far real but uneven.
The main risk is the disappearance of entry-level roles through which young professionals learn, which could leave firms without future senior staff.
AI may reduce differences between workers within firms but widen inequality between firms and between labour and capital.
Governments should not resist AI but guide it through serious retraining, better social protection for career changes and strict competition policy.
Firms should use AI to enhance their employees rather than replace them, while workers should cultivate human skills such as judgement and communication.
The final impact of AI is not predetermined but will depend on political, business and educational decisions and on how its gains are shared.

resumen_modelo: In this opinion piece, the author considers whether generative AI will empty out professional, office-based employment. Anxiety about automation, once confined to manual workers, now affects lawyers, accountants and analysts, and the writer regards it as only partly warranted. What distinguishes the new technology is its capacity to handle non-routine, language-based tasks, which leaves a substantial portion of middle-class work exposed. Nevertheless, exposure differs from job destruction: occupations are made up of varied tasks, and lower costs may actually stimulate demand, as the growth in accountants after the spreadsheet illustrates. Moreover, organisations adopt innovations slowly, so the productivity gains observed so far are genuine but patchy. The genuine threat, the author contends, lies elsewhere: by eliminating junior positions, firms could dismantle the training ground for future senior staff, while the benefits may be captured by a few technology giants and shareholders rather than employees. Consequently, public authorities ought to steer rather than block the technology, through rigorous retraining, social insurance that facilitates career changes and vigilant competition rules. Companies, for their part, should use AI to enhance their workforce, and individuals should cultivate distinctly human abilities. Ultimately, the outcome will hinge on collective choices rather than on the machines themselves.

preguntas.enunciado: Indica si la afirmación es verdadera (V), falsa (F) o si el texto no lo dice (ND).
preguntas.pregunta: The author believes that the fears of white-collar workers are completely unfounded.
preguntas.cita: Are their fears justified? Partly, I would argue, but not in the way most people imagine.
preguntas.explicacion: El autor dice que los temores están justificados «en parte», aunque no por los motivos que la gente imagina. No los considera infundados.

preguntas.pregunta: What makes large language models different from previous waves of automation?
opciones: They mainly replace manual work in factories
They can perform non-routine work based on language
They are cheaper than earlier machines
respuestas: They can perform non-routine work based on language
preguntas.cita: they encroach on precisely the kind of non-routine, language-based work that economists once considered safe
preguntas.explicacion: La novedad es que afectan al trabajo no rutinario basado en el lenguaje. Sustituir trabajo manual o seguir reglas explícitas es lo que hacían las automatizaciones anteriores; el coste no se menciona.

preguntas.enunciado: Busca en el párrafo 1 una palabra que signifique «invaden, se adentran en (un terreno ajeno)».
preguntas.pregunta: Find a word meaning 'gradually intrude on'.
preguntas.cita: they encroach on precisely the kind of non-routine, language-based work
preguntas.explicacion: «To encroach on» significa invadir poco a poco un terreno que pertenece a otro; aquí, el terreno del trabajo cualificado.

preguntas.enunciado: Indica si la afirmación es verdadera (V), falsa (F) o si el texto no lo dice (ND).
preguntas.pregunta: According to the text, clerical and administrative jobs seem to be the most exposed to AI.
preguntas.cita: Clerical and administrative roles appear the most vulnerable, followed by jobs in finance, law and marketing.
preguntas.explicacion: El texto dice expresamente que los puestos administrativos parecen los más vulnerables, por delante de finanzas, derecho y marketing.

preguntas.pregunta: What does the example of spreadsheets illustrate?
opciones: That cheaper analysis can increase demand for a profession
That accountants were replaced by software
respuestas: That cheaper analysis can increase demand for a profession
preguntas.cita: the number of accountants grew, because cheaper analysis created an appetite for more of it
preguntas.explicacion: El ejemplo muestra que abaratar un servicio puede aumentar su demanda y, con ella, el empleo. Precisamente desmiente que la tecnología destruya siempre empleo o que sustituyera a los contables.

preguntas.enunciado: Indica si la afirmación es verdadera (V), falsa (F) o si el texto no lo dice (ND).
preguntas.pregunta: Early surveys show that AI has already doubled productivity in most companies that use it.
preguntas.cita: productivity gains that are real but unevenly spread
preguntas.explicacion: Las encuestas muestran resultados irregulares y ganancias reales pero desiguales; no se habla de duplicar la productividad. La afirmación exagera y es falsa.

preguntas.pregunta: Why could cutting junior positions be harmful for firms in the long run?
respuestas: Because junior tasks are how young professionals learn their job; without them, firms will lack trained people able to take on senior roles in the future.
preguntas.cita: they may save money today only to discover tomorrow that nobody is ready to step into senior positions
preguntas.explicacion: El autor señala que las tareas sencillas son la escuela de los profesionales jóvenes; suprimirlas ahorra a corto plazo pero rompe la cantera de futuros directivos.

preguntas.enunciado: Busca en el párrafo 5 una expresión que signifique «adormecernos en la autocomplacencia, hacernos bajar la guardia».
preguntas.pregunta: Find an expression meaning 'make us feel falsely safe'.
preguntas.cita: None of this, however, should lull us into complacency.
preguntas.explicacion: «To lull someone into complacency» es dar a alguien una falsa sensación de seguridad que le hace bajar la guardia.

preguntas.enunciado: Indica si la afirmación es verdadera (V), falsa (F) o si el texto no lo dice (ND).
preguntas.pregunta: AI assistants seem to benefit less experienced workers more than experienced ones.
preguntas.cita: AI assistants raise the productivity of less experienced workers the most, narrowing the gap between novices and veterans
preguntas.explicacion: Según los primeros estudios citados, los asistentes de IA elevan sobre todo la productividad de los menos experimentados, lo que reduce la distancia con los veteranos.

preguntas.pregunta: Which policy does the author NOT recommend?
opciones: Serious retraining linked to real vacancies
Restricting the use of AI to protect existing jobs
Reforming social insurance for mid-career changes
respuestas: Restricting the use of AI to protect existing jobs
preguntas.cita: Resisting the technology would be futile and probably self-defeating
preguntas.explicacion: El autor rechaza resistirse a la tecnología por inútil y contraproducente. Las otras tres medidas son precisamente las que propone.

preguntas.enunciado: Indica si la afirmación es verdadera (V), falsa (F) o si el texto no lo dice (ND).
preguntas.pregunta: The senior manager quoted by the author works for a technology company.
preguntas.explicacion: El texto cita a «un alto directivo» sin indicar el sector de su empresa. No se puede saber si trabaja en una tecnológica.

preguntas.enunciado: Busca en el párrafo 9 una palabra que signifique «anticuadas, tradicionales».
preguntas.pregunta: Find a word meaning 'traditional, belonging to the past'.
preguntas.cita: are, by and large, old-fashioned ones
preguntas.explicacion: «Old-fashioned» significa anticuado o tradicional; el autor subraya la paradoja de que las competencias más valiosas sean las de siempre.

preguntas.pregunta: What does the author mean by saying 'the outcome is not written in the code'?
respuestas: The author means that the technology itself does not determine the consequences for employment; they will depend on decisions taken by governments, companies and educators, and on how the gains are distributed.
preguntas.cita: It will depend on choices made in parliaments, boardrooms and classrooms over the coming decade
preguntas.explicacion: La metáfora rechaza el determinismo tecnológico: el resultado depende de decisiones humanas y del reparto de las ganancias de productividad.

tribunal.pregunta: What is the main thesis defended by the author?
tribunal.pista_es: Resumir la tesis en dos o tres frases.
ideas: AI will reshape rather than destroy white-collar work
the real risks are fewer junior roles and unequal gains
outcomes depend on policy choices

tribunal.pregunta: Why does the author distinguish between 'exposure' and 'destruction'?
tribunal.pista_es: Explicar la diferencia entre tareas y empleos.
ideas: jobs are bundles of tasks
automation of some tasks may complement others
elasticity of demand can increase employment

tribunal.pregunta: Have you used AI tools in your studies or work? How did they change the way you work?
ideas: drafting and summarising
need to check accuracy
time saved for higher-value tasks

tribunal.pregunta: How could AI affect the Spanish labour market, given its structure?
tribunal.pista_es: Relacionar con la estructura productiva española (servicios, pymes, paro juvenil).
ideas: large share of services and SMEs with slow adoption
high youth unemployment and risk to entry-level jobs
public administration as a potential user

tribunal.pregunta: Do you agree that Europe should not try to slow down the technology?
tribunal.pista_es: Dar una opinión razonada sobre regulación e innovación.
ideas: the EU AI Act as a risk-based approach
risk of falling further behind the US and China
regulation can build trust and protect rights

tribunal.pregunta: What role should competition policy play in the AI economy?
tribunal.pista_es: Relacionar con concentración de mercado y plataformas.
ideas: few firms control models, data and computing power
risk of gatekeepers and abuse of dominance
Digital Markets Act and merger control

tribunal.pregunta: If AI raises productivity, why might wages not rise accordingly?
tribunal.pista_es: Analizar el reparto entre trabajo y capital.
ideas: bargaining power of workers
market concentration and rents
gains captured by owners and shareholders
role of taxation and social dialogue

glosario.nota: «Rung» es el peldaño de una escalera de mano; se usa para jerarquías.
De «to hollow out», vaciar por dentro; muy usado para el empleo de cualificación media.

glosario.nota: Término usado en la Ley de Mercados Digitales de la UE.
